newsitem.title: UK: Strong UK spending calls for restraining rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Strong UK spending calls for restraining rate rise.

text.p: Solid UK retail sales in October and an explosive leap in money supply growth put the spotlight firmly back on the interest rate debate, analysts said.

A shock quarter-point base rate rise in October is unlikely to be enough to choke off rampant consumer spending although a tight budget from Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke next week could relieve some of the pressure.
"This will increase the pressure on the Chancellor to tighten monetary policy pre-election," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident.
Clarke will deliver his budget on November 26 with most economists expecting some tax cuts -- about three billion pounds-worth in total -- as elections are only six months away.
Retail sales rose 0.4 percent in October, translating to year-on-year growth of 4.1 percent. But given that they dropped 0.3 percent in September, a consumer boom still looks some way off.
"Spending has cooled down from the rapid pace seen over the summer," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "Sales continue to trend upwards but fears of a consumer boom are overdone."
More worrying for the monetary policy hawks was a leap in broad money supply growth. M4 jumped to 10.3 percent year-on-year in October, from 9.9 in September.
The government has a three-to-nine percent monitoring range for M4. It has rarely ducked below the top of that range in recent times.
As a result, although the Bank of England has often highlighted the inflationary implications of strong money supply growth, M4 has not been a priority policy indicator for Clarke.
But with M4 lending also shooting up, soaring to 7.4 billion stg in October, he may have to sit up and take notice now.
Economists noted October's huge 4.4 billion stg repayment of public sector debt should have depressed M4. So the underlying picture may be even stronger than the headline figure suggests.

"Even the non-monetarists will recognise the danger signals in such high rates of monetary growth," said CIBC Wood Gundy's chief economist David Coleman. "But a tough, credible budget next week still offers Mr Clarke his best chance of avoiding a politically damaging increase in base rates," he said.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, said official retail sales figures continued to paint a less robust picture than anecdotal evidence.
For example, the British Retail Consortium's latest sales monitor showed UK retail sales up 5.9 percent year-on-year in value terms in October.

And Coleman noted that even though retail sales growth was moderate last month, there were pockets of real strength on the high street. Textile, clothing and footwear sales were up 1.0 percent in the month and 9.1 percent year-on-year and non-food sales were 5.8 percent higher than on a year earlier.
"For the budget, it can be argued that giving more money to the consumer is the last thing you should do. But I expect the consumer will get some more anyway," Shepperd said.

Shepperd said an increasing number of players in the bond and money markets were tipping another rate rise to result from the December 11 monetary meeting between Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
"That may be too early, but it is a question of when, not if," he said, forecasting a quarter-point rate rise before elections due by May 1997, taking base rates to 6.25 percent.

"The last thing the consumer needs is another shot in the arm from tax cuts," said Alex Garrard, economist at UBS. "If the Chancellor duly obliges next Tuesday, there is unlikely to be an early let-up in the chorus calling for a new year rate rise."
